content: The references provided are a comprehensive collection of studies, reviews, and guidelines related to the diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease, particularly in the context of HIV-infected individuals. 1. A systematic review of the literature on cryptococcal meningitis was conducted, highlighting the burden of the disease and its management strategies. (Clin Infect Dis. 2018;66:1122–32) 2. Garcia-Hermoso et al. provided epidemiological evidence supporting the existence of dormant Cryptococcus neoformans infections, which may later reactivate under immunosuppressive conditions. (J Clin Microbiol. 1999;37:3204–9) 3. Mitchell and Perfect reviewed the history of cryptococcosis, particularly its emergence as a significant opportunistic infection in the era of AIDS, 100 years after the discovery of Cryptococcus neoformans. (Clin Microbiol Rev. 1995;8:515–48) 4. Speed and Kaldor reported the rarity of cryptococcal infections in children, emphasizing the need for further research into pediatric cases. (Pediatr Infect Dis J.) 5. Gonzalez et al. described the clinical presentation and outcomes of cryptococcosis in HIV-infected children, underscoring the challenges in managing this population. (Pediatr Infect Dis J.) 6. Meiring et al. compared pediatric-onset and adult-onset cryptococcosis cases using population-based surveillance data from 2005–2007, revealing differences in disease presentation and outcomes. (AIDS. 2012;26:2307–14) 7. Loyse et al. called for urgent action to improve global access to flucytosine, a 50-year-old antifungal critical for treating cryptococcosis. (J Antimicrob Chemother. 2013;68:2435–44) 8. Lightowler et al. evaluated the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, highlighting the challenges of resource-limited settings. (PLoS One) 9. Kambugu et al. analyzed outcomes of cryptococcal meningitis in Uganda before and after the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), demonstrating improved survival rates. (Clin Infect Dis. 2008;46:1694–701) 10. Bicanic et al. investigated the relationship between cerebrospinal fluid pressure, fungal burden, and patient outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis, emphasizing the importance of serial lumbar punctures. (AIDS. 2009;23:701–6) 11. Graybill et al. provided guidelines for diagnosing and managing increased intracranial pressure in AIDS patients with cryptococcal meningitis, a critical aspect of care. (Clin Infect Dis. 2000;30:47–54) 12. Rolfes et al. demonstrated that therapeutic lumbar punctures significantly reduce acute mortality in cryptococcal meningitis patients. (Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59:1607–14) 13. Likasiwattanakul et al. described the clinical features and outcomes of cryptococcosis in HIV-infected children in Southeast Asia. (Southeast Asian J Trop Med Public Health) 14. Abadi et al. reviewed cases of cryptococcosis in children with AIDS, highlighting the unique challenges in this demographic. (Clin Infect Dis.) 15. Finanga et al. conducted a trial in Tanzania and Zambia to evaluate the impact of cryptococcal meningitis screening and early adherence support in advanced HIV patients starting antiretroviral therapy. (Lancet. 2015;385:2173–82) 16. Govender et al. updated the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society guidelines for preventing, diagnosing, and managing cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals. (South Afr J HIV Med. 2019;20:1030) 17. Ford et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the optimal CD4 cell count threshold for cryptococcal antigen screening in HIV-infected individuals. (Clin Infect Dis. 2018;66(Suppl. 2):S152–9) 18. Awotiwon et al. reviewed the role of primary antifungal prophylaxis in preventing cryptococcal disease in HIV-positive individuals. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;8:CD004773) 19. Jarvis et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of cryptococcal antigen screening as a strategy to prevent HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis in South Africa. (PLoS One. 2013;8:e69288) 20. Cassim et al. assessed the cost-per-result of laboratory-based reflex cryptococcal antigenemia screening in HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts in South Africa. (PLoS One. 2017;12:e0171675) 21. Chipungu et al. explored the feasibility and acceptability of cryptococcal antigen screening in a resource-limited HIV/AIDS clinic in Malawi. (PLoS One. 2015;14:387–90) 22. Meya et al. demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of serum cryptococcal antigen screening to prevent deaths among HIV-infected individuals with low CD4 counts in resource-limited settings. (Clin Infect Dis. 2010;51:448–55) 23. Rajasingham et al. advocated for integrating cryptococcal antigen screening and preemptive treatment into routine HIV care. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr.) 24. Smith et al. reported on the prevalence of cryptococcal antigenemia and the cost-effectiveness of a cryptococcal antigen screening program in Vietnam. (PLoS One. 2013;8:e62213) 25. Vidal et al. identified a high prevalence of asymptomatic cryptococcal antigenemia in hospitalized HIV-infected patients in São Paulo, Brazil. (Trop Med Int Health. 2016;21:1539–44) 26. Hakim et al. evaluated enhanced prophylaxis combined with antiretroviral therapy for advanced HIV infection in Africa, showing improved outcomes. (N Engl J Med. 2017;377:233–45) 27. Parkes-Ratanshi et al. conducted a randomized trial in Uganda to assess the efficacy of fluconazole as primary prophylaxis for cryptococcal disease in HIV-positive adults. (Lancet Infect Dis. 2011;11:933–41) 28. Leenders et al. compared liposomal amphotericin B with conventional amphotericin B for treating AIDS-associated cryptococcal meningitis, demonstrating improved safety and efficacy. (AIDS. 1997;11:1463–71) 29. Hamill et al. conducted a randomized trial comparing two doses of liposomal amphotericin B and conventional amphotericin B for acute cryptococcal meningitis treatment. (Clin Infect Dis. 2010;51:225–32) 30. Botero Aguirre et al. reviewed the effects of amphotericin B deoxycholate versus liposomal amphotericin B on kidney function, highlighting the nephrotoxicity of the former. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;11:CD010481) 31. Beardsley et al. investigated the role of adjunctive dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, finding no significant benefit. (N Engl J Med. 2016;374:542–54) 32. Eshun-Wilson et al. compared early versus delayed antiretroviral therapy initiation in HIV-positive individuals with cryptococcal meningitis, emphasizing the importance of timing. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;(7):CD009012) 33. Sun et al. addressed the management of cryptococcal meningitis with extremely high intracranial pressure in HIV-infected patients, emphasizing the need for aggressive intervention. (Clin Infect Dis. 2004;38:1790–2) 34. Meda et al. described an operational research study in Tanzania using strict schedules of serial lumbar punctures for managing cryptococcal meningitis. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2014;66:e31–6) 35. Perfect et al. provided updated clinical practice guidelines for managing cryptococcal disease, emphasizing evidence-based approaches. (Clin Infect Dis. 2010;50:291–322) 36. Newton et al. conducted a randomized trial of acetazolamide for treating elevated intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningitis, finding limited efficacy. (Clin Infect Dis. 2002;35:769–72) 37. Haddow et al. proposed clinical case definitions for cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in HIV-1-infected individuals. (Lancet Infect Dis. 2010;10:791–802) 38. Larson et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening HIV-infected patients with low CD4 counts for cryptococcal antigenemia before initiating antiretroviral therapy. (PLoS One. 2016;11:e0158986) 39. Vallabhaneni et al. assessed the implementation of a public-sector cryptococcal antigen screening and treatment program in South Africa, demonstrating feasibility and impact. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2016;72:e37–42) 40. Rick et al. explored the operational challenges and outcomes of cryptococcal antigen screening programs in resource-limited settings.
